name: Soukous Cavacha
desc: The driving cavacha groove at the root of soukous, with a continuous sixteenth-note hi-hat carpet, syncopated kick, and a clave-derived snare backbeat. Popularized by Zaiko Langa Langa in the 1970s.

name: Soukous Sebene
desc: Fast dance-section (sebene) kit groove driving the interlocking guitar riffs of soukous, with anticipated tresillo-leaning kick and open-hat lift on the offbeats.

name: Rumba Lingala
desc: Classic mid-tempo Congolese rumba groove descended from Cuban son, with relaxed two-feel kick, steady eighth hi-hat, and a son-clave-referencing snare. The lingala-language ballroom style of the 1950s-60s.

name: Ndombolo
desc: High-energy modern descendant of soukous with an emphatic dance-led kick driving the floor under razor-sharp sebene guitars; sixteenth-note hat and hard backbeat.

name: Kwassa Kwassa
desc: The mid-1980s Kanda Bongo Man dance variant of soukous, a lilting cavacha derivative with swaying hip-led groove and syncopated kick.

name: Makossa
desc: Cameroon's brisk 4/4 dance groove with a bottle-percussion offbeat, interlocking rhythm guitar and anticipated bass, made global by Manu Dibango.

name: Bikutsi
desc: Cameroon's intense 6/8 (12/8) Beti groove built on a 4-over-3 cross-rhythm, with a four-on-the-floor pulse cutting against the continuous triple hi-hat; name means beating the ground.

name: Assiko
desc: Bassa guitar-and-bottle dance music of coastal Cameroon, a brisk 4/4 with a clinking metal-on-bottle offbeat and lively syncopated snare fills.

name: Afrobeat (Tony Allen Pattern 1)
desc: Tony Allen's foundational afrobeat groove for Fela Kuti: a loose, jazz-and-highlife-informed 4/4 with broken kick, displaced ghost snares and an offbeat open-hat shimmer.

name: Afrobeat (Tony Allen Pattern 2)
desc: A denser Tony Allen afrobeat variation with a continuous sixteenth-note hi-hat and conversational kick-snare interplay underpinning Fela's horn sections.

name: Afrobeats (Pop)
desc: The modern Lagos pop groove (Wizkid/Davido era) blending a tresillo-derived kick with a relaxed backbeat and shaker-like hat; descended from afrobeat and dancehall.

name: Juju
desc: Yoruba guitar-band dance music (King Sunny Ade) over a lilting 12/8 with talking-drum and shekere; the kit follows the standard bell time-line.

name: Fuji
desc: High-energy Yoruba percussion music (Barrister, Kollington) driven by bata, sakara and dundun talking drums in a dense 12/8 over the standard bell.

name: Apala
desc: Contemplative Yoruba Muslim percussion style (Haruna Ishola) with sekere, agidigbo thumb-piano, agogo bell and talking drums over a 12/8 bell at 85-110 BPM.

name: Highlife (Nigerian)
desc: Nigerian highlife's bright 4/4 dance groove with asymmetrical Yoruba-derived kick figures and syncopated guitar; the gentleman's dance-band sound of the 1950s-60s.

name: Highlife (Ghanaian)
desc: The Ghanaian dance-band highlife groove with a swinging offbeat open-hat, relaxed two-feel kick, and clipped offbeat guitar; rooted in palm-wine and brass-band traditions.

name: Palm-Wine (Osibisaba)
desc: Relaxed acoustic guitar-and-percussion social music of the Akan coast, the rural seed of highlife, with sparse two-feel kick and clip-bottle backbeat.

name: Hiplife
desc: Ghanaian fusion of highlife melody and hip-hop programming, with a tresillo-derived 808 kick and crisp backbeat clap; the Reggie Rockstone sound of the 1990s.

name: Mbalax (Sabar Kit)
desc: Senegal's national popular style (Youssou N'Dour) translating polyrhythmic Wolof sabar drumming to the kit, with rapid snare flurries and accented offbeat kick.

name: Mbalax Accompaniment
desc: The core mbalax accompaniment part, the basic timekeeping figure a sabar drummer masters first, rendered on kit with dense ghost-snare strokes evoking the talmbat bass drums.

name: Baar (Sabar)
desc: Baar, a Wolof sabar dance rhythm, with its characteristic syncopated accent pattern adapted to drum kit; the snare voices the open and slap sabar strokes.

name: Ceebu Jen (Sabar)
desc: Ceebu jen, a popular sabar dance rhythm named after the Senegalese national rice-and-fish dish, with a buoyant accented figure carried by snare and kick.

name: Kaolack (Sabar)
desc: Kaolack, a fast Wolof sabar rhythm named after the Senegalese city, with off-beat anticipated kick and rolling ghost-snare ornaments.

name: Wassoulou
desc: Southern Mali's Wasulu hunters' music (Oumou Sangare) over buoyant 6/8 cross-rhythms with kamele ngoni and percussion, the kit tracking the standard bell.

name: Bambara (Bamana)
desc: Bamana djembe-and-dunun ensemble feel of central Mali adapted to kit, dense interlocking 12/8 with the bell time-line and accented support-drum strokes on snare.

name: Chimurenga (Mbira)
desc: Thomas Mapfumo's chimurenga, translating interlocking mbira dzavadzimu cycles to band instruments over a dense 12/8 with hosho-shaker pulse and the standard bell.

name: Nhemamusasa (Mbira)
desc: The core Shona mbira repertoire piece Nhemamusasa (building a shelter) rendered as a 12/8 cyclical groove with hosho-derived shaker accents and a four-pulse foundation.

name: Jit
desc: Fast Zimbabwean guitar dance music translating mbira patterns to electric guitar over a driving four-on-the-floor 4/4 pulse with crisp backbeat.

name: Sungura
desc: Zimbabwe's rapid guitar-band style blending Congolese rumba/soukous with local feels, with a galloping kick and offbeat open-hat under busy lead guitar.

name: Mbaqanga
desc: South African township jive with a driving shuffle, cyclical bass ostinato, choppy offbeat guitar and a swinging open-hat; the Mahlathini and Mahotella Queens sound.

name: Marabi
desc: The 1920s-30s Johannesburg shebeen keyboard style with a rolling 12/8 swing, repeating I-IV-V cycle and shaker pulse; ancestor of mbaqanga and South African jazz.

name: Kwela
desc: Pennywhistle street jive of 1950s townships with a brisk walking-bass shuffle and skiffle-like offbeat; the lilting precursor to mbaqanga.

name: Kwaito
desc: Soweto's slowed-down house (100-120 BPM) with a four-on-the-floor kick, offbeat open-hat and deep bass; the post-apartheid township pop of the 1990s.

name: Amapiano
desc: South Africa's slow (108-115 BPM) house-jazz-kwaito hybrid with a four-on-the-floor kick, rolling offbeat shaker-hats and rim/clap backbeat; the bass is the syncopated log drum.

name: Amapiano Log Drum
desc: The defining amapiano feel from the log-drum's perspective: a syncopated woody bass that bounces between the four-on-the-floor kick (here on hhFoot) rather than landing on it.

name: Gqom
desc: Durban's dark, minimal broken-beat house with a tresillo-driven, off-kilter kick (no steady four-on-the-floor), heavy sub-bass and tribal chant; ancestor of 3-step.

name: 3-Step
desc: A contemporary South African club style with a distinctive three-kick-drum pattern per bar instead of four-on-the-floor, blending amapiano's log-drum bounce with UK broken beat.

name: Shangaan Electro
desc: Nozinja's hyper-fast (up to 190 BPM) Afro-futurist Tsonga dance music, a marimba-led reboot of Tsonga disco with rapid-fire kineticism and minimal bass.

name: Benga
desc: Luo guitar dance music of western Kenya with interlocking guitar ostinati, a bouncing bass and crisp 4/4 backbeat; crystallized in the 1960s from nyatiti lyre traditions.

name: Taarab
desc: The sung poetry orchestra music of the Swahili coast (Zanzibar/Mombasa), blending Arab, Indian-film and Cuban influences over a gentle chakacha-derived dumbak groove.

name: Chakacha
desc: The hip-swaying Swahili wedding ngoma of coastal Kenya and Tanzania, with a sensuous tresillo-driven dumbak/conga groove underlying taarab-style melodies.

name: Bongo Flava
desc: Tanzania's Swahili hip-hop/R&B pop blending mid-tempo hip-hop beats and dancehall riddims with taarab and rumba DNA; a tresillo-flavored kick under smooth melodies.

name: Semba
desc: Angola's foundational 4/4 dance music (86-100 BPM) with anticipated bass placed before the downbeat, accented offbeats and dikanza scraper; ancestor of samba and kizomba.

name: Kizomba
desc: Angola's slow, sensual partner-dance music (70-90 BPM) with the kick on beats one and three forming a steady heartbeat under zouk-derived synths and syncopated percussion.

name: Kuduro
desc: Angola's frenetic (140-150 BPM) electronic dance music with a fast four-to-the-floor kick and a sidestick/snare sounding the first two hits of the tresillo, plus chopped shouts.

name: Funana
desc: Cape Verde's accordion-driven (gaita) dance music with a relentless ferrinho scraper carrying a continuous sixteenth pulse over a fast two-beat drive.

name: Coladeira
desc: Cape Verde's upbeat, satirical 4/4 dance song-form, a faster and more syncopated cousin of morna with an anticipated bass and lively backbeat.

name: Morna
desc: Cape Verde's slow, melancholic national song-form (Cesaria Evora) in a gentle 4/4 with sparse two-feel bass and brushed backbeat evoking saudade.

name: Batuque
desc: The oldest Cape Verdean genre from Santiago island, a women's call-and-response built on cloth-bundle (tchabeta) thigh-slapping in a driving, polyrhythmic groove.

name: Gnawa
desc: Moroccan Sufi trance music with a gimbri bass establishing one motive against the qraqeb iron-castanet semiquaver pulse, producing the characteristic 3:2 hemiola in 12/8.

name: Chaabi (Moroccan)
desc: Moroccan popular wedding music in a buoyant 6/8 (12/8) where the rhythm starts on the high-pitch percussion and the bass falls late in the cycle, adapting bendir frame-drum patterns.

name: Nuba Basit
desc: The opening, stately movement of the Andalusi nuba suite, whose broad mizan (rhythmic cycle) anchors the slow introductory sung sections of Moroccan al-ala.

name: Nuba Qaim wa Nusf
desc: The qaim wa nusf (one-and-a-half) mizan of the Andalusi nuba, a measured asymmetric cycle marking the second movement of the suite.

name: Nuba Btayhi
desc: The btayhi mizan, a flowing duple cycle forming the third movement of the Andalusi nuba as the suite gathers momentum.

name: Nuba Darj
desc: The darj (stair/gradual) mizan, the fourth and increasingly lively movement of the Andalusi nuba in a rolling triple feel.

name: Nuba Quddam
desc: The quddam (forward), the fast concluding movement of the Andalusi nuba, a dance-like 6/8 that brings the suite to its energetic climax.

name: Malouf
desc: The Tunisian branch of Andalusian classical music, its nuba progressing from slow introductions to lively dance-like endings over measured mizan cycles played on tar and darbouka.

name: Rai
desc: Algeria's Oran-born popular music (Khaled, Cheb Mami) over a tresillo-driven darbouka/kit groove with a 3-3-2 kick and hard backbeat under raspy vocals.

name: Chaabi (Algerian)
desc: The Algiers Casbah popular song style (El Hadj M'Hamed El Anka) blending Andalusi modes with a swinging 6/8 derbouka-and-tar accompaniment.

name: Egyptian Maqsum
desc: The maqsum, the most common rhythm of Egyptian popular and bellydance music: a duple cycle with dum on 1 and the and-of-2, and tek on the backbeat, played on tabla/darbouka.

name: Egyptian Baladi
desc: The baladi rhythm of Egyptian shaabi/folk dance, a maqsum variant with a heavy double-dum opening (dum-dum on 1) giving it an earthy downtown Cairo feel.

name: Sudanese Tom-Tom (Daluka)
desc: The Sudanese 'tom-tom' or daluka hand-drum groove underpinning haqiba and modern Khartoum pop, a swung 6/8 blending Arabic and Nilotic African feels.
